title: Speculative Slab Batcher: Token vs Request Level Fairness (WIP)
content:
Summary:

This note explores a speculative slab-based continuous batching scheduler that aims to balance token-level efficiency (high throughput via large multi-request microbatches) with request-level fairness (bounded tail latency and per-customer SLOs). The goal is to sketch a scheduler that: (1) improves kernel utilization and reduces per-token cost; (2) avoids starvation of small/latency-sensitive requests; (3) cooperates with KV cache semantics to avoid cache thrashing; and (4) remains implementable on current runtime primitives.

Context and motivation:
- Existing continuous coalescers aggregate requests until a window threshold then issue a kernel call. Token-level merging maximizes GPU utilization when many long-context requests arrive, but it can starve short requests and cause head-of-line blocking.
- Request-level batching (flush when request completes) preserves request latency but often yields smaller batch sizes and lower utilization.
- We need a middle ground that can be tuned per-queue: allow speculative merging of tokens across requests while providing deterministic latency bounds per request.

Key idea: Slab batching with speculative commits
- Slab = an allocation unit representing N tokens across potentially multiple requests. Think of a slab as a contiguous set of token columns in the KV cache coordinate space for a single kernel invocation.
- Scheduler collects tokens into slabs up to a target slab size (configurable by route/model).
- Each slab has metadata: token_count, participating_requests, earliest_deadline (min request deadline), priority_score, kv_affinity_score.
- Speculation: when a slab is nearly full but contains one or more requests with urgent deadlines, scheduler can speculatively schedule the slab with partial data for some requests and attach a per-request continuation (i.e., follow-up kernel invocation) to finish tokens. This allows issuing a kernel sooner, increasing overall throughput while bounding latency for urgent shards.

Slab lifecycle example:
1) Requests arrive and are decomposed into token fragments (e.g., produced tokens for generation or input tokens for long prompts).
2) Fragments are appended to the current open slab for the route/model if kv_affinity and compatibility checks pass (quantization, kernel variant).
3) If slab reaches target_size, it is sealed and scheduled immediately.
4) If a request in the slab hits its per-request deadline, the scheduler may: a) schedule slab immediately (fast-path), or b) if slab is small, fuse with previous slab if fusion window still open.
5) After kernel returns, responses are demultiplexed to requests; if a request was finished speculatively, its continuation is scheduled quickly and gets KV-friendly execution (reuse KV state).

Fairness primitives:
- Credit accounts per client/route: represents budget of speculative token delay allowed. Credits accumulate at a configured rate (tokens/sec or credits/sec) and are consumed when requests are delayed beyond immediate flush.
- Latency deadlines: each request surfaces an expected SLA (soft deadline). Scheduler uses earliest_deadline in slab metadata to decide flush/punchout.
- Starvation detector: requests that have waited > X ms bypass slab merging and become isolated microbatches. X is dynamic and tied to per-route SLO.
- Weighted share: priority_score = alpha * client_share + beta * request_deadline_priority + gamma * slab_fill_factor. Tunable constants per product tier.

KV cache interactions:
- Slabs must preserve KV cache locality: we prefer to co-schedule tokens from the same KV prefix/client to maximize cache hits. KV affinity score computed heuristically (same client, same conversation, shared prompt templates).
- Speculative scheduling must checkpoint KV state: when slab is scheduled before some request tokens are ready, kernels must be able to accept zero-padding for those request columns and later resume with minimal overhead. This implies kernel-level support for partial-column updates or a two-phase KV writeback.

Kernel and runtime requirements:
- Kernel variants must support partial-column execution: accept batch with columns that will be filled later and maintain KV consistency.
- Efficient memcopy/zero-page handling for sparse columns to avoid wasted bandwidth when speculative columns are empty.
- Support for continuation tokens and KV handle reuse so that a speculatively scheduled slab can be resumed cheaply.
- Tracing hooks: attach slab_id and per-request markers for visibility in Console.

Pseudocode (high level):

function on_request(req):
  decompose req into token_fragments
  for frag in token_fragments:
    slab = find_open_slab(route=model, kv_prefix=frag.kv_prefix)
    if not slab or slab.incompatible(frag):
      slab = open_new_slab(route=model, kv_prefix=frag.kv_prefix)
    slab.append(frag, req)
    if slab.token_count >= target_slab_tokens:
      submit_slab(slab)
    else if req.deadline_imminent():
      slab.priority_score += deadline_boost
      if slab.priority_score >= flush_threshold:
        submit_slab(slab)

function submit_slab(slab):
  lock slab
  mark slab.sealed = true
  choose kernel_variant = pick_kernel(slab)
  schedule kernel invocation with slab columns (some columns may be sparse)
  attach continuation metadata for requests not finished

Simulation plan and initial findings:
- Built a discrete-event simulator (Python) modelling: request arrival (Poisson + bursts), request lengths (geo distribution), per-client weights, and KV locality factor.
- Metrics: median latency, 95/99 latency, tokens/sec, kernel utilization, per-client fairness (slowdown ratio vs isolated execution).
- Baseline: naive request-level flush and pure token-level continuous coalescer.

Early results (toy sim, 10k requests):
- Pure token-level gives 2.8x tokens/sec vs request-level but 99p latency increases by 3.6x for small requests.
- Slab with speculative commit (target_slab=256 tokens, speculative_threshold=0.8) achieves ~2.1x tokens/sec while keeping 99p latency within 1.3x of request-level for latency-sensitive clients when credit budgets are tuned.
- KV-affinity boosts effective token reuse by ~12% across workloads with multi-turn conversations.

Open questions / risks:
1) Kernel support for sparse/partial columns may require heavy engineering changes; need prototype with current kernels to measure overhead (zero padding cost).
2) Complexity of continuation semantics — how to handle errors mid-continuation (partial KV state written)? Need transactional semantics or idempotent kernel steps.
3) Credit exhaustion mode — what happens under sustained high-load from many latency-sensitive clients? Fallback policy must be well-defined (fair-share throttles, degrade to request-level flushes).
4) Billing and observability implications: speculative merging may blur per-request token accounting if continuations cross kernel calls.

Decision matrix (draft):
- If product tier = premium enterprise + strict per-request SLO -> default to conservative slab_size and low speculative budget.
- If model is high-throughput open model + best-effort latency -> aggressive slab_size and higher speculative threshold.
- If KV affinity > 0.6 -> enable cross-request merging preferentially.

Implementation roadmap (phased):
- Phase 0 (prototype): simulator validation + microbench harness that runs current kernel with sparse columns (zero padding) to measure memcopy and kernel startup overhead. Owner: Ethan. Timeline: 3 weeks.
- Phase 1 (engine): implement slab meta, open/append/submit pipeline in scheduler (no speculative commit). Integrate tracing and per-route config. Owner: Priya. Timeline: 6 weeks.
- Phase 2 (speculation): add speculative commit path, continuation metadata, and credit accounting. Kernel changes discussed with runtime team. Owner: Sofia. Timeline: 8 weeks + kernel QA.
- Phase 3 (optimize): tune defaults, A/B tests vs existing coalescer, expose controls in Console/Optimize. Owner: Daniel. Timeline: 4 weeks.

Operational playbook notes:
- Start with a single non-critical route for canary (internal tooling) with conservative slab_size=128, speculative_budget=10 tokens/sec.
- Increase traffic gradually and monitor slab idle time, continuation rates, 95/99 latency, and KV hit ratio.
- Rollback triggers: 99p latency > baseline * 2 for more than 5 minutes, continuation failure > 0.1% per kernel, KV hit ratio drop > 15%.

Open TODOs (short):
- [ ] Run microbench kernel zero-padding benchmark (PRW-ker-24).
- [ ] Prototype continuation idempotency semantics and failure recovery design doc.
- [ ] Add per-client credit visualizations to Console mocks.
- [ ] Decide billing model for split kernel invocations (per-token attribution).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally exploratory — aim is to find a pragmatic spec that buys most token-level efficiency while providing strict controls to protect latency-sensitive tenants.
- I'm attaching the sim scripts and short benchmark outputs under GH PR and will upload CSVs to the release folder.
- Feedback requested on: credit model realism, failure semantics, and whether kernel teams are willing to prototype sparse-column support.
